title: Sirianni’s Decision Sparks Jaguars’ Little to Nail Dramatic Game-Winning Kick on ESPN】
body:
Philadelphia head coach Nick Sirianni publicly shouldered the blame for the strategic decisions that preceded the Jacksonville Jaguars’ dramatic, last‑second field‑goal victory in London on Sunday, a 19‑17 loss that left the Eagles’ playoff hopes hanging in the balance. The Eagles, who had held a two‑point lead with just seconds remaining, chose to run a short, conservative play that set up Jaguars kicker Riley Little’s 46‑yard winner, a decision that Sirianni later described as “the wrong call at the wrong time.” The defeat not only snapped Philadelphia’s three‑game winning streak but also thrust the team into a precarious position in the NFC East as the regular season heads into its critical final stretch.

The game, played at the iconic Wembley Stadium, was a showcase of contrasting styles. Philadelphia’s offense, led by quarterback Jalen Hurts, had been methodical all night, moving the ball efficiently and converting on key third‑down opportunities. Yet, after a hard‑fought defensive stand that forced Jacksonville to punt with 1:12 left, Siriann i elected to have the offense line up in a formation that limited the clock’s runoff. Instead of attempting a deeper pass to the end zone—a play that could have secured a two‑point conversion and forced overtime—the Eagles opted for a quick slant to wide receiver DeVonta Smith, who was tackled just short of the goal line. The ball was spotted at Jacksonville’s 18‑yard line, leaving the Jaguars ample time to set up a field‑goal unit.

Critics quickly pointed out that the decision ignored both statistical trends and the situational context. In the NFL, teams trailing by two points with under a minute left convert at a higher rate when they attempt a pass into the end zone rather than a short run, especially when the defense is fatigued. Moreover, the Eagles’ offensive line had been dominant all night, allowing Hurts to drop back and release a clean pass without significant pressure. By choosing a low‑risk, low‑reward play, Sirianni effectively handed Jacksonville a chance to regroup. The Jaguars capitalized, advancing the ball to the 31‑yard line before Little’s kick sailed through the uprights, sealing the win.

The fallout extends beyond a single loss. Philadelphia entered the game at 6‑3, perched second in the NFC East behind the New York Giants, who hold a 7‑2 record. A win would have moved the Eagles to the top of the division and given them a tiebreaker edge. Instead, the defeat dropped them to a tie with the Washington Commanders, intensifying the race for the final playoff berth. The loss also exposed lingering concerns about Sirianni’s play‑calling under pressure. While his overall record this season remains respectable—13‑5 in regular‑season games—this particular decision has reignited debates about his willingness to trust his offense in clutch moments.

Inside the locker room, the mood was a mixture of disappointment and resolve. Hurts, who finished with 242 passing yards and a rushing touchdown, addressed the media after the game, stating, “We made a mistake, and we own it. We’ll learn from it and get better.” Veteran linebacker Haason Reddick echoed the sentiment, emphasizing that the team must “stay focused on the next game” and not let the London loss define their season. The coaching staff, meanwhile, has reportedly begun reviewing the final series in detail, with an eye toward adjusting timeout usage and play selection in future close‑game scenarios.

Looking ahead, the Eagles face a daunting schedule that includes back‑to‑back matchups against the Dallas Cowboys and the New York Giants, both of whom are vying for the same division crown. The next two weeks will be a litmus test for Sirianni’s ability to adapt his game‑management philosophy and for the roster to rebound from a demoralizing defeat on foreign soil. If Philadelphia can translate its offensive firepower into decisive late‑game execution, the team still has a realistic path to the postseason. However, the London loss serves as a stark reminder that in the NFL’s razor‑thin margins, a single call can swing momentum—and fortunes—by inches.
